## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

Also trigger for cleaning or restructuring messy tabular data files (malformed rows, misplaced headers, junk data) into proper spreadsheets. The deliverable must be a spreadsheet file. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved.

Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.

=== decisions.txt tail ===
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
D-11  T-610: how is the system demonstrated at the viva?
      TASKLIST: "Decide this now, not the night before."
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
A 60-paper run is 20-40 minutes on CPU against a rate-limited free tier. That
cannot be run live in front of an examiner.

OPTIONS
  (a) Pre-bake a full showcase run that replays instantly, and demo LIVE only
      at max_papers=10.  [RECOMMENDED - this is what TASKLIST specifies]
      Removes every live-network dependency from the graded moment while still
      proving the thing genuinely runs. Justify it as demo RELIABILITY, not as
      a latency workaround.
  (b) Fully live.
      One rate-limit or network hiccup and the demo dies in front of the
      committee.
  (c) Fully pre-baked, nothing live.
      Safe, but invites "did it actually run?" and you have no answer in the
      room.

ANSWER: a


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
D-12  T-705: who does the 50-claim spot-check, and when?
      Affects: your only in-domain non-circular evidence
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Human-only, cannot be delegated to the pipeline (the whole point is that it is
independent of the pipeline). Even with T-325 in hand, this is the only
verifier measurement taken in YOUR domain - SciReviewGen is biomedical-and-CS
survey prose; your corpus is agentic RAG. TASKLIST: "Both are needed; they
answer different objections."

It needs real pipeline output, so it cannot start before M1 (Aug 31 target).

# ResearchGPT — Master Task List

> **What this file is.** The single executable backlog for the whole project, derived from `PROJECT_PLAN.md`, `RESEARCHGPT_SPEC.md`, `SESSION_CONTEXT.md`, `ARCHITECTURE_REVIEW.md` and the two `diagrams/*_EXPLAINED.md` files.
>
> **Two-agent workflow.** **Claude Code plans, specifies, reviews and integrates. Cursor (Groq) writes the code.** Every task below is written so it can be handed to Cursor as a self-contained unit of work with a hard acceptance test.
>
> **Companion documents:** `TRAINING_SPEC.md` (both fine-tuned models — verifier and reranker — and why the generative agents are not trained), `DB_SCHEMA.md` (the Postgres run registry), `PROJECT_PLAN.md` (scope), `SESSION_CONTEXT.md` (constraints and literature findings).
>
> Created 2026-08-25. Update the checkboxes in place; do not rewrite the file.

---

## 0. Reality check — read this before anything else

| | |
|---|---|
| Plan written | 2026-08-06 (30-day plan, Day 1 = 2026-08-07) |
| Today | **2026-08-25** |
| Target submission | **~2026-09-07** (was ~09-05; +2 days authorised 2026-08-25 to integrate SciReviewGen) |
| Days actually remaining | **13** |
| Code written so far | **Zero.** No `src/`, no `pyproject.toml`, no `.py` file anywhere in the folder. |

**The 30-day plan is no longer executable as written.** Nineteen of its thirty days are gone and none of them produced code. What exists is planning, literature, design and two graded decks.

This file is therefore **not** the 30-day plan re-typed. It is a compressed 11-day plan that applies the descope ladder in `PROJECT_PLAN.md §10` **up front** rather than in a panic on Day 28. Concretely, the following are cut before starting, not deferred:

| Cut now | Was | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Ollama feasibility probe | §6.3 | Already demoted to a footnote. Dead. |
| DOCX writer | §2.2 | Markdown + PDF-from-Markdown suffices. |
| 2-annotator Likert + Cohen's κ | §9 | Scheduling cost exceeds its evidentiary value at 11 days. Replaced by the 50-claim spot-check. |
| Ablations 3 and 4 | §9.4 | Kept only if Phase 7 finishes early. **Ablation 2 is never cut.** |
| Extraction F1 annotation (10 papers) | §5.4 | Replaced by 5 qualitative examples. |

**Reinstated 2026-08-25: SciReviewGen is back in scope (Phase 3B).** The original cut rested on a premise that turned out to be false — `PROJECT_PLAN.md §5.3` assumed distribution "as preprocessing scripts over S2ORC, historically requiring an AI2 access request with days of latency." **Three ungated public mirrors exist on Hugging Face** (`kejian/SciReviewGen`, `kdercksen/scireviewgen-csv`, `pat-jj/SciReviewGen`), verified downloadable 2026-08-25. There is no access request and no lead time. Two days were authorised for the integration; the schedule absorbs them at the back (§13).

**Never cut, under any circumstance** — these seven are the project: the six agents, the trained **verifier** (the reranker fine-tune in Phase 3C is a *second* trained model and is explicitly droppable — see T-335), the evidence-inspection panel, ablation 2 (− Verifier), `trace.jsonl`, the **M1 milestone** (first complete cited survey), the **SciReviewGen verifier cross-check (T-325)**, and — as of the 2026-08-25 decision — **Human-in-the-Loop (T-609)**.

> If M1 has not landed by **2026-08-31**, stop building forward and stabilise what exists. A working four-agent pipeline that produces a cited survey beats a half-wired six-agent graph that runs nothing.

---

## 0.1 Model policy — HARD RULE, no exceptions ★

**Only free, open-weight models. No paid models, no paid tiers, no trial credits, at any point in this project.**

This is Constraint 1 from `SESSION_CONTEXT.md §2` and it is not negotiable. If a task cannot be done on the allowlist below, the task gets descoped — the budget does not get raised.

### Allowlist — verified live on 2026-08-25

Every generative agent (Planner, Extractor, Critic, Writer) runs on one of these. All are **open-weight** models on a **free tier**, so the project is $0 by construction rather than by discipline.

| Model | Provider | Weights | Verified | Use for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `gemma-4-31b-it` | Google AI Studio | open | ✅ HTTP 200, extracted correctly | **Primary candidate** — all four agents |
| `gemma-4-26b-a4b-it` | Google AI Studio | open (MoE, ~4B active) | ⚠️ HTTP 200 but returned `{}` on the extraction probe | Speed fallback only; re-test before use |
| `openai/gpt-oss-120b` | Groq | open (Apache 2.0) | ✅ HTTP 200 | **Primary backup** — largest free open-weight option |
| `openai/gpt-oss-20b` | Groq | open (Apache 2.0) | not yet probed | Lightweight fallback |
| `qwen/qwen3.6-27b` | Groq | open | ✅ HTTP 200 | Second backup / bake-off arm |

...
- [ ] **T-904** 🧠 Keep the `trace.jsonl` schema stable from T-107 onward. Every report figure depends on it.

---

## 12. Critical path

Only these gate M2. Everything else can slip.

```
T-001/002 ─▶ T-104 (llm.py + cache) ─▶ T-201..210 (retrieval) ─▶ T-212 (recall gate ≥ 0.80)
                                                                        │
T-301 ─▶ T-302 ─▶ T-303 (Kaggle) ─▶ T-304 (ONNX int8) ──────────┐      │
        (parallel, unattended)                                    │      ▼
                                                                  │  T-402..407 ─▶ 🔴 M1 (Aug 31)
T-320 ─▶ T-321 ⛔ ─▶ T-322 ─▶ T-323 ─▶ T-324 ────────┐            │                    │
        (Phase 3B — parallel data track, no API,      │            │                    │
         no pipeline, does NOT gate M1 or M2)         │            └──▶ T-501..507 ─────┴─▶ 🔴 M2 (Sep 2)
                                                       │                                     │
                                                       │                       T-603 (fixture) ─▶ T-607 (Panel 3)
                                                       │                                     │
                                       T-304 ─────────▶ T-325 ★★ ──▶ T-705b ◀── T-705   T-702 (Ablation 2)
                                              (verifier cross-check)      (three-lens table)

T-330 ─▶ T-331 ─▶ T-332 (Kaggle) ─▶ T-333 ─▶ T-334 ─▶ T-335 (adoption gate)
        (Phase 3C — reranker fine-tune. NOT on the critical path at all:
         the pipeline ships with the stock reranker and T-335 is a weight
         swap. A failed run here costs nothing downstream.)

Phase 3B joins the critical path only at T-325, which needs the trained verifier.
Everything before it is independent parsing work. T-321 is the internal blocker:
if the bib-resolution gate fails, T-322..T-325 cannot proceed.

Phase 3C touches the critical path nowhere. It reuses T-321's parser and
T-212's eval harness, and its output is optional by construction (T-335).

Phase 6B (Postgres registry) is likewise off the critical path by design: the
pipeline writes to disk regardless and T-625 falls back to a filesystem scan.
```

---

## 13. Kill switches — decide these on the date, not in hindsight

| Date | If this has not happened | Do this |
|---|---|---|
| **Aug 28** | Recall@20 < 0.80 | Escalate `bge-small` → `bge-base`. Spend all of Aug 29 on retrieval. Push M1 to Sep 1. |
| **Aug 28** | T-321 bib-resolution gate < 0.95 | The delimiter parse is wrong. Spend half a day fixing it. If it still fails, fall back to **`kdercksen/scireviewgen-csv`** (same splits) before abandoning — do not lose T-325 to one bad mirror. |
| **Aug 29** | Kaggle verifier not trained | Fall back to a **stock** NLI checkpoint in the pipeline and report stock-vs-tuned as future work. The pipeline must never block on training. |
| **Aug 30** | T-322 pairs not produced | Drop the T-324 retrieval gold sets (T-212b) and keep **only** the T-325 cross-check. The cross-check is why this track exists; the retrieval breadth check is a bonus. |
| **Aug 30** | Reranker fine-tune (T-332) not trained, or T-334 shows no out-of-domain gain | **Keep the stock reranker and move on.** The pipeline is unaffected — this was always a weight swap, never a dependency. Report the negative result; a fine-tune that did not help is an honest finding, and the verifier still satisfies the training requirement on its own. |
| **Aug 31** | M1 not landed | **Stop building forward.** Stabilise the linear pipeline, ship the survey, cut the Critic loop to a single pass. |
| **Sep 2** | M2 not landed | Ship the five-agent system without the Critic loop. **The Verifier stays** — it is the graded component; the loop is not. |
| **Sep 4** | Vue not started | Ship Panels 1–3 against the fixture, **plus the minimum HITL surface** — a dropped-claims list with confirm/override writing to `human_overrides`. ⚠️ **HITL can no longer be dropped (T-007, 2026-08-25).** Cut Panel 4's *styling and artefact-download chrome* instead, not its function. |
| **Sep 4** | Phase 6B registry not working | **Cut it entirely.** `GET /api/runs` falls back to a filesystem scan and loses nothing the demo needs — the filesystem already holds everything the registry would store. Revert the deck to Chroma + SQLite instead (`SESSION_CONTEXT.md §7.2`). |
| **Sep 6** | Ablations not run | Ship ablation 2 alone. It is the graded claim. Report the rest as future work. |

---

## 14. Open items only you can close

Carried forward from `SESSION_CONTEXT.md §8`, plus new ones. All appear in Phase 0 or Phase 8 above; repeated here so none is lost:

1. **T-005** — confirm the base-paper switch with your guide. ⬅ *the most valuable ten minutes left*
2. **T-006** — confirm which MCD notation the rubric means.
3. **T-007** — decide whether HITL stays in Objective 2.
4. **T-811** — obtain the Li et al. IPM PDF and resolve its publication year.
5. **T-812** — verify *Vicinagearth* is Scopus-indexed.
6. **T-705** — the 50-claim spot-check. Nobody else can do it. *It is no longer your **only** non-circular evidence now that T-325 exists, but it is still the only one measured in **your own domain** — SciReviewGen is biomedical-and-CS survey prose, your corpus is agentic RAG.* Both are needed; they answer different objections.

---

*Derived from `PROJECT_PLAN.md` (rev 3), `RESEARCHGPT_SPEC.md`, `SESSION_CONTEXT.md`, `ARCHITECTURE_REVIEW.md`, `LITERATURE_REVIEW.md`, `PAPER_DEEP_DIVE.md`, and the 2026-08-09 and 2026-08-20 sessions. Amend in place.*

=== configs/default.yaml ===
# ResearchGPT — default run configuration
#
# Typed by src/researchgpt/core/models.py::RunConfig. Unknown keys are rejected.
#
# NOTE: this file deliberately does NOT follow RESEARCHGPT_SPEC.md §10.1's
# `llm:` block. That block names gpt-4o-mini and gpt-4o, which are forbidden
# under TASKLIST §0.1 ($0, free open-weight models only). The spec's config
# predates the zero-budget constraint.
#
# T-004 BAKE-OFF: COMPLETE (2026-08-25). 5 real gold-set abstracts per arm,
# through the real extractor_v1 prompt and the real LLMClient.
#
#   arm                   parse valid fields echo   avg lat   verdict
#   openai/gpt-oss-120b    100%  100%  4.6/8    0     26.6s   PRIMARY
#   qwen/qwen3.6-27b       100%  100%  7.0/8  2/5     41.8s   rejected
#   gemma-4-31b-it            -     -      -    -         -   disqualified
#   gemma-4-26b-a4b-it        -     -      -    -         -   disqualified
#
# WHY gpt-oss WINS DESPITE LOWER FIELD COVERAGE:
#   qwen echoed the literal schema placeholder "string" into datasets/metrics
#   on 2 of 5 papers (40%). That is the worst possible failure mode here: it
#   parses, it validates, and it silently injects fabricated content into a
#   hallucination-graded pipeline (SPEC §14.2 forbids exactly this).
#   qwen's 7.0/8 field score is itself INFLATED by the echo - excluding the
#   echoed rows it scores 6.33/8. gpt-oss echoed 0/5.
#
# KNOWN WEAKNESS OF THE WINNER: gpt-oss populates only 4.6/8 content fields.
#   This is most likely a PROMPT problem, not a model problem - extractor_v1
#   ships 3 few-shot examples and Dagdelen et al. measured structured output
#   stabilising at ~20. T-404 must expand the few-shots, then re-run this
#   bake-off and expect the field count to rise.
#
# LATENCY REALITY CHECK (TASKLIST §0.2 tolerance is ~30 min/run):
#   gpt-oss ~26.6s/paper x ~70 papers = ~31 min for the extraction stage
#   alone. Right at the tolerance. The response cache makes re-runs free, but
#   the FIRST full run will sit near 30-40 min end to end.
#   Groq latency is highly variable under load (measured 3.8s-55s same arm).

llm:
  model: openai/gpt-oss-120b       # Extractor / Critic / Writer — 27x faster
  planner_model: openai/gpt-oss-120b   # Planner
  temperature: 0.1
  max_tokens: 4096
  requests_per_minute: 15          # free-tier throttle (T-104)
  max_retries: 5
  cache_dir: data/llm_cache        # prompt-hash cache (T-104)

embeddings:
  model: BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5    # CPU-sized, down from bge-large
  device: cpu
  batch_size: 32

retrieval:
  dense_k: 30
  sparse_k: 30
  fusion: rrf
  rrf_k: 60
  rerank: true
  # T-335 REVERTED 2026-08-27 after the first real pipeline run (M1).
  #
  # The tuned SciReviewGen reranker WAS adopted, on the measured condition that
  # "the live pool is 98.2% on-topic, so there is little for a miscalibrated
  # model to mis-promote". That condition was drawn from T-212's CACHED pool,
  # built from 15 hand-written, tightly-scoped queries. The Planner (T-402)
  # generates 20+ broader queries, and the resulting pool is far more
  # heterogeneous - so the measurement did not generalise.
  #
  # Observed in M1 output: the tuned model's top-10 contained edge-server RL,
  # IoT monitoring and US biodiversity specimens. A/B on the same live pool,
  # query "multi agent retrieval literature review":
  #     stock  #1 LiRA (multi-agent literature review)          +7.77
  #     tuned  #1 "real-time behavioral monitoring in IoT"      +4.77
  #                LiRA demoted to #2                           +2.10
  #
  # The relevance control (T-335) flagged exactly this and was right. Keeping
  # the stock model until the reranker is retrained with MIXED negatives
  # (~3 hard : 1 random) - training on 100% BM25 hard negatives is what removed
  # its ability to recognise irrelevance (T-331).
  reranker: cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2   # ~22M, CPU. Stock: calibrated.
  final_k: 12
  chunk_size: 1200
  chunk_overlap: 200

sources:
  # OpenAlex is the mandatory primary (reliable, keyless, rich venue/OA data).
  # Semantic Scholar reinstated 2026-08-25 (TASKLIST §0.2): claimed on 8 slides
  # of the Review-2 deck, and its rate limiting is survivable now that latency
  # is not a constraint. It is BEST-EFFORT — on sustained 429s the run
  # continues on openalex + arxiv. Crossref stays cut (redundant).
  # Semantic Scholar DISABLED 2026-08-27 (decision: use OpenAlex instead).
  #
  # Why: keyless it answers roughly 1 query in 3 and burns up to 60s of
  # exponential backoff on each miss (decisions.txt D-03 chose to skip the free
  # academic key). Measured on the first M1 attempt: that alone was ~16 minutes
  # of pure sleeping across a 24-task plan, and the run was killed at 10 min
  # having completed 38 of 72 source-queries.
  #
  # TASKLIST 0.2 requires "OpenAlex OR Semantic Scholar" - OpenAlex satisfies
  # it, and OpenAlex is now keyed (1,000 searches/day, 0.2) so there is ample
  # headroom without S2.
  #
  # ⚠️ The T-214 connector is NOT deleted and still passes its tests. Both decks
  # claim Semantic Scholar on 8 slides, so say "implemented and available,
  # disabled by default for latency" rather than removing the claim (T-809).
  # Re-enable by adding semantic_scholar back to this list - ideally once
  # S2_API_KEY exists (T-215), which removes the throttling entirely.
  enabled: [openalex, arxiv]
  max_per_source: 25

review:
  min_papers: 20
  # Lowered 60 -> 25 on 2026-08-28. Extraction is one sequential LLM call per
  # paper and the 6-example prompt made each slower, so 60 papers is ~60-90 min
  # against the ~30-minute tolerance in TASKLIST 0.2. 25 is also the size
  # TASKLIST already specifies for ablation runs (T-702/T-703), so the flagship
  # run and the ablations are now directly comparable rather than differently
  # sized.
  #
  # ⚠️ Consequence for T-409's recall figure: with a 35-paper answer key, the
  # CORPUS recall ceiling is 25/35 = 0.714. It cannot reach 0.80 at this
  # setting, by arithmetic, and must not be read as a retrieval failure.
  # UNION recall - did retrieval find the paper at all - is unaffected, and
  # decisions.txt D-04 already makes that the primary gate for exactly this
  # reason.
  max_papers: 25
  year_min: 2019
  max_iterations: 3                # hard cap, forced WRITE on the last
  grounding_threshold: 0.7
  coverage_threshold: 0.8

verifier:
  onnx_path: data/models/verifier-int8.onnx
  tokenizer: microsoft/deberta-v3-small
  support_threshold: 0.7           # biased to precision (T-503)

output:
  citation_style: ieee
  formats: [markdown, csv, bibtex]
  runs_dir: outputs/runs

# Literature Review: How do multi-agent retrieval-augmented systems reduce hallucination in automated literature review?

## Methods and Architectures

### 3.1 Methodological Trends in Multi‑Agent Architectures for Knowledge‑Intensive Tasks 

Recent work on multi‑agent systems (MAS) for complex information‑processing problems converges on three complementary design axes: **training‑execution coordination**, **modular specialization**, and **information‑propagation control**. 

| Design axis | Representative approaches | Core methodological idea |
|-------------|---------------------------|--------------------------|
| **Centralized training / decentralized execution (CTDE)** | MAPPO for edge‑server monitoring | A Multi‑Agent Proximal Policy Optimization algorithm is trained centrally while each dispatcher executes its learned query‑and‑dispatch policy using only locally stale observations, thereby reconciling global optimality with on‑device autonomy【1】. |
| **Modular agent specialization** | LiRA literature‑review framework; MARS misinformation detector; CoTHSSum summarizer | Separate agents are assigned distinct sub‑tasks (e.g., outlining, fact‑checking, style analysis, hierarchical segmentation) and their outputs are later fused by a “judge” or decoder, enabling parallel reasoning and richer feature fusion【2】【12】【5】. |
| **Information‑propagation control via topology design** | EIB‑LEARNER topology; SAFE‑CARE benchmark layers | A causal framework evaluates how sparse versus dense communication graphs affect error diffusion, leading to a hybrid topology that balances robustness and bandwidth cost【11】; the benchmark isolates the impact of adding retrieval, guardrails, or memory layers on safety and user experience【8】. |

#### 3.1.1 CTDE versus Fully Decentralized Policies 

CTDE remains attractive for domains where global performance metrics (e.g., throughput‑cost trade‑offs) are hard to observe locally. MAPPO demonstrates that centralized policy gradients can be leveraged without requiring each agent to maintain a full view of the system state【1】. In contrast, fully decentralized reinforcement learning often suffers from non‑stationarity and limited credit assignment, prompting researchers to embed lightweight coordination mechanisms (e.g., periodic state broadcasts) as an alternative to full CTDE【7】. The survey on agentic LLMs notes that “retrieval enables tool use” and that “reflection improves multi‑agent collaboration,” suggesting that decentralized agents can compensate for limited training signals by augmenting inference with external knowledge sources【7】.

#### 3.1.2 Specialized Agent Pipelines 

LiRA’s pipeline partitions the literature‑review task into outlining, subsection drafting, editing, and final review agents, each fine‑tuned on a dedicated sub‑dataset (SciReviewGen and a proprietary ScienceDirect corpus)【2】. A similar modular philosophy underlies MARS, which deploys four domain‑specific agents (Fact Checker, Emotion Analyzer, Intent Recognizer, Style Analyzer) to extract orthogonal features before a cross‑agent review and a final Judge Agent synthesize the verdict【12】. CoTHSSum extends this idea to long‑form summarization by first segmenting documents hierarchically and then applying chain‑of‑thought prompting within each segment, yielding interpretable intermediate reasoning steps that are later combined through structure‑guided decoding【5】. Across these systems, the common advantage is **parallelizable reasoning** and **transparent intermediate artifacts**, which the Agentic LLMs survey identifies as a cross‑category benefit of multi‑agent collaboration【7】.

#### 3.1.3 Retrieval‑Augmented Interaction 

Retrieval‑augmented generation (RAG) appears both as a stand‑alone pipeline (e.g., an academic‑services chatbot that builds a domain‑specific knowledge base via hierarchical chunking and query reranking【10】) and as an auxiliary layer in multi‑agent setups (e.g., the retrieval component in SAFE‑CARE that isolates its safety impact【8】). Qlarify introduces *recursively expandable abstracts*, allowing users to iteratively request deeper context while the system retrieves and synthesizes additional passages on demand【4】. These approaches share the premise that **dynamic information retrieval can reduce the need for exhaustive model memorization**, a point echoed in the Agentic LLMs survey’s observation that “retrieval enables tool use”【7】.

#### 3.1.4 Topology‑Driven Information Diffusion 

The effectiveness of multi‑agent communication is not solely a function of agent competence but also of the underlying graph structure. EIB‑LEARNER proposes a hybrid topology that fuses dense connectivity (to promote beneficial information spread) with sparse links (to suppress error propagation), achieving lower communication cost and higher robustness in empirical evaluations【11】. The SAFE‑CARE benchmark complements this line of work by providing a controlled ablation environment where the addition or removal of a single architectural layer (e.g., memory or profile write‑back) can be directly linked to changes in safety and user‑experience metrics【8】. Together, these studies illustrate a **design tension**: dense graphs maximize knowledge sharing but increase the risk of cascading mistakes, whereas sparse graphs improve fault tolerance at the expense of slower convergence.

#### 3.1.5 Synthesis and Open Disagreements 

- **Training coordination**: While CTDE (MAPPO) is praised for achieving superior system‑level trade‑offs, the Agentic LLMs survey cautions that centralized training may limit scalability and adaptability in rapidly evolving domains【1】【7】. 
- **Modularity versus end‑to‑end learning**: Specialized pipelines (LiRA, MARS, CoTHSSum) report qualitative gains in interpretability and cross‑domain performance, yet the survey highlights that “reflection improves multi‑agent collaboration,” implying that end‑to‑end reflective mechanisms could replace explicit modularization in some settings【2】【12】【5】【7】. 
- **Topology design**: EIB‑LEARNER’s hybrid graphs are shown to outperform both purely dense and purely sparse configurations, but the SAFE‑CARE benchmark reveals that the *optimal* topology may be task‑dependent, as safety‑critical layers sometimes require denser communication to propagate guardrails effectively【11】【8】.

Overall, the emerging consensus is that **methodological diversity—spanning CTDE, modular specialization, retrieval augmentation, and topology engineering—offers a richer toolbox for building robust, scalable multi‑agent systems**. Future research will need to reconcile these strands, perhaps by developing adaptive architectures that can switch between centralized and decentralized modes, reconfigure agent specializations on the fly, and dynamically adjust communication graphs in response to observed error patterns.

Caught up. Here's where things actually stand — the memory I had was badly stale ("zero code"), so I've rewritten it.

## The project

**ResearchGPT** — GRIET DSC06 major project, submission ~2026-09-07 (**10 days left**). A six-agent RAG pipeline that writes a *cited* literature survey and uses a trained NLI verifier to drop claims it can't ground. Hard constraint: **$0, free open-weight models only** (Groq `gpt-oss-120b` primary, enforced by an `ALLOWED_MODELS` check in `core/llm.py`).

Working split: **Claude Code plans/specs/reviews, Cursor+Groq writes code, you do the 👤 tasks.** `TASKLIST.md` is the backlog (update checkboxes in place); `decisions.txt` holds your answers to D-01..D-16.

## What happened since 25 Aug

Three days took it from zero code to a working pipeline. **58 of 116 tasks done, 164 tests passing, 12 commits, working tree clean.**

| Phase | State |
|---|---|
| 0–2 core + retrieval | ✅ |
| 3 verifier train | ✅ macro-F1 **0.516 → 0.769** on SciFact |
| 3B SciReviewGen | ✅ cross-check, 38.3% agreement on human citations |
| 3C reranker | ✅ trained, **adopted then reverted** |
| 4 agent graph | ✅ **M1 landed 27 Aug, 4 days early** |
| 5 Verifier + Critic | ❌ not started |

The reranker revert is the interesting one: it passed its out-of-domain gate (nDCG@10 +0.030, Recall@20 +0.167) on a *cached* pool from 15 hand-written queries, then failed on the live Planner-generated pool — it promoted "real-time behavioral monitoring in IoT" over LiRA on a multi-agent literature-review query. Root cause: 100% BM25 hard negatives in training removed its ability to recognise irrelevance. The fix (mixed ~3 hard : 1 random negatives, retrain, ~40 min) is what you said you'd do "tomorrow" — that's today.

## Three things open, in priority order

**1. Phase 5 is the whole point and hasn't started.** T-501..T-509 — claim decomposition, the ONNX verifier wrapper, verdict thresholds, claim dropping, the Critic loop. M2 is due Sep 2. Everything else remaining is polish next to this; it's the graded centrepiece and the reason the architecture exists.

**2. T-409 flagship run** — ready, never started (I stopped it at your word). One 25-min run at `max_papers=25` yields three deliverables: the report's survey chapter (T-807), the pre-baked demo (T-610), and the **T-212 recall number Phase 2 has been blocked on since 26 Aug** (baseline union recall was 0.371 against a 0.80 gate; the Planner was supposed to be the fix, and this measures whether it worked).

**3. The 12 commits are local-only.** `master` is 12 ahead of `origin/master` — Phases 2 through 4 including M1 exist on this disk and nowhere else, invisible to both co-authors.

## One thing I noticed reading the M1 output

The survey reads well, but the corpus behind it is thin: **12 papers, 9 references, and every single one `text_availability: none`** — abstract-only. Off-topic papers made it in (edge-server MAPPO, IoT monitoring). That matters because T-505 says abstract-only papers *may not supply verified claims* — Li et al. measured abstract-conditioned faithfulness at 0.745 vs 0.94–0.96 with full context. If the flagship corpus stays abstract-only, the Verifier will have very little it's allowed to ground against. Worth watching when T-409 runs properly.

Want me to start on Phase 5, or run T-409 first?

  |---|---|
  | chapters | 3,000 sampled from a 20,000-row pool |
  | **distinct surveys** | **1,381** (2.2 chapters per survey) |
  | unique cited abstracts | 13,929 |
  | **pairs** | **75,395** — 15,079 positive / 60,316 negative, exactly **1:4** |

  ⚠️ **Sequential reading would have wrecked survey diversity.** Chapters of one survey sit adjacent in the parquet, so the *first* N rows span almost no surveys — measured: **150 rows → 13 surveys**. Sampling across a 20,000-row pool instead gives **1,381 surveys from 3,000 chapters**. Survey diversity is precisely what the reranker has to generalise over, so this is not a cosmetic change.

  *Fewer pairs than `TRAINING_SPEC`'s ~120k estimate (75k) because the mean chapter cites ~5 papers, not the 8-per-chapter cap.* Ample for a 22M cross-encoder.
- [x] **T-331** ⌨️ ★ **BM25 hard-negative mining** — for each query take BM25 top-50 from the pooled split corpus, drop true positives, sample at 1 positive : 4 negatives. *Done when: a spot-check of 20 negatives confirms they are topically plausible, not random.* ⚠️ **Hard negatives are the whole point. Random negatives make the task trivial — the model learns topic matching, which BM25 already does, and stock-vs-tuned will show no gain. If T-334 shows ~0 improvement, suspect this task first.** ✅ **DONE 2026-08-27, and the diagnostic this warning asks for is now built in.**

  | | |
  |---|---|
  | BM25 depth mined | top-50 |
  | mean hard candidates per query | **47.6** |
  | queries short of hard negatives | **0** |
  | **random-fallback negatives** | **0 (0.0%)** |

  **Every negative in the training set is a genuine BM25 hard negative** — a document BM25 already ranks highly and is wrong about. Nothing was padded at random.

  ★ **`random_fallback_share_of_negatives` is recorded in `eval/rerank_triples_t330.json` specifically so T-334's null result, if it comes, is diagnosable rather than mysterious.** If that share is high, BM25 could not find confusable documents and the model was handed a task it could already do. On this build it is 0.0, so a null T-334 would *not* be explained here — look at the training config or accept the honest negative.

  Regression-tested: a true positive can never be sampled as a negative for its own query, and a corpus too small to supply negatives emits **fewer** rather than inventing them, flagging the shortfall.
- [x] **T-332** 🧠 Kaggle notebook: `cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2`, binary cross-entropy, max_len 512, lr 2e-5, batch 32, 2 epochs, fixed seed. *Expect 20–30 minutes on a T4.* **Train the verifier (T-303) first — it is the graded component and takes priority on the quota.** ✅ **NOTEBOOK DONE 2026-08-27** — `notebook-kaggle-traning/02_train_reranker_scireviewgen.ipynb` (17 cells) + README section. **The verifier ran first and passed T-307 at 0.769, so the quota is free.**

  **Smoke-tested, not just written.** All 8 code cells were executed locally on CPU against a 600-pair subset — data load, survey-grouped split, CrossEncoder build, stock baseline, `fit()`, the ranking comparison and save all ran clean.

  ⚠️ **One thing the smoke test nearly hid.** Stock and fine-tuned printed *identical* metrics to four decimals, which looks exactly like a no-op trainer. Verified directly that `CrossEncoder.fit()` does mutate the model — raw scores moved by up to **3.49** — so the identical metrics were coarse metrics over 2 dev queries, not broken training. *Worth knowing before someone reads a flat table on Kaggle and concludes the run failed.*

  🔴 **FAILED ON THE FIRST REAL KAGGLE RUN, and it is a failure the local CPU smoke test could not have caught.** `AttributeError: 'DataParallel' object has no attribute 'preprocess'` — Kaggle's **GPU T4 x2 exposes two devices**, so `sentence-transformers` wraps the model in `torch.nn.DataParallel`, and `BinaryCrossEntropyLoss` then calls `self.model.preprocess(...)`, which the wrapper does not forward. Training dies partway through `model.fit()`. *No single-GPU or CPU test can reproduce this; it needs two visible devices.*

  **Fixed** by setting `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0` as the very first statement of section 1 — **before torch initialises CUDA** — plus an assert in section 2 that only one device is visible. A 22M cross-encoder gains nothing from a second GPU; DataParallel would mostly add transfer overhead. ⚠️ On recurrence the kernel must be **restarted**: the pin has no effect once CUDA is initialised.

  ⚠️ **This notebook needs a data upload**, unlike the verifier one: BM25 hard-negative mining needs the whole pooled corpus, so `data/rerank/train_triples.jsonl` (~99 MB) must be attached as a Kaggle Dataset. The notebook globs `/kaggle/input/**/train_triples.jsonl`, so the dataset name does not matter. Steps are in the README.
- [x] **T-333** ⌨️ ONNX export + int8 dynamic quantization, matching the verifier's deployment path. *Done when: the quantized model reproduces float logits within tolerance and per-query CPU latency is measured.* **HARNESS DONE 2026-08-27, awaiting the trained checkpoint** — `src/researchgpt/rerank/export_onnx.py`.

  ⚠️ **The stated criterion — "reproduces float logits within tolerance" — is the wrong test for a *reranker*.** Only the induced **ordering** matters: a model whose scores all shift by a constant ranks identically and is perfectly usable. So the export checks (a) ONNX fp32 vs PyTorch on raw scores, which is the genuine *export-correctness* test, and (b) **Kendall tau ≥ 0.9** for int8, which asks whether quantization *reshuffled the ranking* rather than whether it moved the numbers.

  ✅ **RUN 2026-08-27 on both checkpoints: PASS.** fp32 vs PyTorch max |Δscore| **5e-6**; int8 **Kendall τ 0.960** (10-epoch) / **0.968** (2-epoch, the shipped build) vs torch, so quantization preserves rank order. Size **91 MB → 23 MB**. *int8 is NOT the problem with this model — tuned-pytorch and tuned-int8 score within ~0.1 of each other throughout.*

  🔴 **`TRAINING_SPEC §2.5` warns "quantization must not be assumed free", and that warning already fired once** — T-304 measured int8 as free on the *stock* verifier (macro-F1 rose 0.516 → 0.539) and then as a 0.027 **loss** on the *fine-tuned* one, dropping it below its own T-307 gate. **A quantization result measured on one checkpoint says nothing about another.** Which graph ships is therefore decided by T-335 on ranking quality, not here.
- [x] **T-334** 🧠 ★ **Stock vs fine-tuned**, on **two** sets: the SciReviewGen `test` split (in-domain) and **your own 25-paper bibliography** (out-of-domain, CS). Report Recall@20, nDCG@10, Precision@12 and rerank latency. *Reuses T-212's harness.* **Lead with the out-of-domain number** — SciReviewGen is frozen mid-2020 and skews biomedical, so a large in-domain gain with no out-of-domain gain means you fitted the benchmark, not the task. **HARNESS DONE 2026-08-27, awaiting the trained checkpoint** — `src/researchgpt/rerank/evaluate.py`.

  **Stock baseline on the out-of-domain set is already measured** (own bibliography, 15 sub-questions, 501 candidates, 19 gold hits pooled):

  | arm | nDCG@10 | Recall@20 | Precision@12 |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | stock `ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2` | **0.2277** | **0.4815** | **0.0926** |
  | fine-tuned | — | — | — |

  **Self-tested**: running the harness with stock in *both* arms returns delta **exactly 0.0000** on all three metrics, so a non-zero delta later is a real difference and not harness noise.

  ✅ **Costs no OpenAlex budget** — it reuses T-212's cached pool (`eval/cache/pool_mps25.json`). That matters now that OpenAlex is metered (§0.2).

  **MEASURED 2026-08-27** against both Kaggle checkpoints, int8 (i.e. what ships). The **2-epoch** build was adopted; the 10-epoch numbers below are near-identical:

  | | stock | fine-tuned | delta |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | **out-of-domain nDCG@10** | 0.2277 | 0.2583 | **+0.0306** |
  | **out-of-domain Recall@20** | 0.4815 | 0.6481 | **+0.1667** |
  | out-of-domain Precision@12 | 0.0926 | 0.0926 | +0.0000 |
  | in-domain nDCG@10 | 0.2646 | 0.7500 | **+0.4854** |

  ⚠️ **The in-domain gain is 16x the out-of-domain gain.** Exactly the pattern this task warns about.

  ⚠️ **And the out-of-domain average hides how thin it is.** Only **9 of 15** sub-questions have any gold paper pooled, and per-query the result is **3 improved, 5 unchanged, 1 regressed** — with the regression losing its only gold paper outright (`scientific information extraction`, Recall@20 1.000 → 0.000). Two of the three "wins" are a single gold paper flipping 0 → 1. *Four queries of evidence.*

  ⚠️ **Harness limitation to state if these latencies are quoted:** the stock arm runs through sentence-transformers/PyTorch and the tuned arm through onnxruntime, so the ms/query column compares **runtimes**, not models. It is not an apples-to-apples latency measurement.
- [x] **T-335** 🧠 **Adoption gate.** Promote the tuned model into `configs/default.yaml` **only if it beats stock on your own bibliography, measured after int8 quantization.** An in-domain-only win is a reportable finding, not a reason to ship. *If it does not pass, keep the stock reranker and report the negative result — that is an honest contribution, and the pipeline is unaffected.* **IMPLEMENTED 2026-08-27** as a mechanical gate in `rerank/evaluate.py`, decided on out-of-domain nDCG@10 and Recall@20.

  🔴 **REVERTED 2026-08-27 by the first real pipeline run (M1). `configs/default.yaml` names the STOCK reranker.**

  The adoption below rested on condition 2 — *the live pool is 98.2% on-topic, so there is little for a miscalibrated model to mis-promote*. **That measurement did not generalise.** It came from T-212's *cached* pool, built from 15 hand-written, tightly-scoped queries. The Planner (T-402) emits 20+ broader queries and produces a far more heterogeneous pool.

  M1's ranked top-10 contained **edge-server RL, IoT monitoring and US biodiversity specimens**. A/B on the same live pool, query `multi agent retrieval literature review`:

  | rank | stock | tuned |
  |---|---|---|
  | 1 | LiRA (multi-agent literature review) **+7.77** | **IoT behavioural monitoring +4.77** |
  | 2 | LatteReview (systematic review) +5.43 | LiRA, demoted to **+2.10** |
  | 3 | MARS (multi-agent retrieval) +5.36 | LatteReview +0.35 |

  **The tuned model ranks an IoT paper above the single most relevant paper in the pool.** The relevance control flagged exactly this and was right; my condition-2 evidence was drawn from an unrepresentative pool. *Two reversals on this decision is not a good look, but the final state rests on production output rather than a proxy, and the lesson is specific: a "the pool is clean" argument must be measured on the pool the PLANNER builds, not on a hand-curated one.*

  <details><summary>Superseded adoption reasoning, kept for the report</summary>

  ✅ **RUN 2026-08-27. VERDICT: PROMOTE WITH CONDITIONS. The tuned reranker is adopted** — `configs/default.yaml` now names `data/models/reranker-onnx` (the **2-epoch**, int8 ONNX build).

  | | stock | **adopted (2-epoch, int8)** | delta |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | **out-of-domain Recall@20** | 0.4815 | **0.6481** | **+0.1667** (+35% rel.) |
  | out-of-domain nDCG@10 | 0.2277 | 0.2577 | +0.0300 |
  | in-domain nDCG@10 | 0.4524 | 0.7828 | +0.3304 |
  | relevance control | **0/15** | **11/15 FAIL** | — |

  **Why the 2-epoch build and not the 10-epoch one:** identical in-domain performance (0.7828 vs 0.7840 — it had converged by epoch 2, so 49 further GPU-minutes moved it −0.001), identical out-of-domain gain, but materially better calibrated (11/15 control violations vs 15/15; off-topic scores +2.9…+5.0 vs +6.8…+9.7). It also matches the 2 epochs `TRAINING_SPEC §2.3` specifies.

  🔴 **The model's ABSOLUTE scores are broken, and it was adopted anyway — deliberately, on measured evidence.** It rates unrelated documents (wind-turbine fatigue, soil nitrogen, opera libretti) at **+3…+5** where stock gives **≈ −11**. Root cause is T-331: *every* negative is a BM25 hard negative from SciReviewGen's own cited-abstract pool, so the model was only ever asked *"which of these topically-adjacent scientific abstracts belongs to this chapter?"*, never *"is this relevant at all?"*. **T-331's warning that "random negatives make the task trivial" is right about necessity but wrong at 100%** — the fix is a mixture (~3 hard : 1 random), not a switch. Not spent; M1 took priority.

  ★ **Two conditions were measured before promoting, and both must keep holding:**
  1. **Nothing consumes the score as a value.** `hybrid_retriever` fuses by **RRF over ranks**; the only other consumer is the eval harness. Enforced in code: `Reranker.filter_by_score()` raises `UncalibratedScoreError` on a fine-tuned model, so a future author reaching for a score cutoff hits a loud explanation instead of a silent bug. **This matters for Phase 5** — if T-506's Critic ever thresholds on retrieval score, it must use the stock model or a recalibrated one.
  2. **The live pool is 98.2% on-topic** (9 of 493 papers clearly off-domain), because T-201 already searches `title_and_abstract` with a date window. On real candidates the tuned model promoted **0** off-topic papers into a top-12, against stock's **1**.

  ⚠️ **RE-RUN THIS GATE if either condition could change** — notably if `max_per_source` rises to 100 (`decisions.txt` D-05), which admits more marginal papers, or if a new source widens the pool.

  ⚠️ **An earlier verdict here read "DO NOT PROMOTE — catastrophically broken". That was an overcorrection and is retracted.** The relevance control was first wired as a hard veto; it measures a real property, but whether that property *matters* depends on the two facts above, which had not been measured when the veto was written. The gate now reports **PROMOTE WITH CONDITIONS** and prints them. *Ranking gains remain a hard requirement — the control cannot rescue a model that does not rank better.*

  </details>

  **Honest reporting line for T-705b / the deck:** *"the fine-tuned reranker raised Recall@20 by 35% on a curated bibliography and improved every in-domain ranking metric, yet we rejected it: a relevance control showed it had stopped recognising irrelevance, and on the first real pipeline run it ranked an IoT-monitoring paper above the most relevant paper in the pool. We traced the cause to training exclusively on BM25 hard negatives."*

  ⚠️ **The gate refuses to be quietly satisfied on the wrong artefact.** Run without `--tuned-onnx` it still reports, but prints that it judged the **unquantized** model and that `TRAINING_SPEC §2.5` requires the decision be made after int8. *That is the exact mistake T-304 made on the verifier — passing a gate on the model that trained rather than the model that ships.*
- [ ] **T-336** 🧠 **UNBLOCKED 2026-08-27** — T-335 adopted the tuned reranker, so this ablation now has two real arms to compare. **Ablation 5 — stock vs fine-tuned reranker**, full system otherwise unchanged, `max_papers=25`. Closes `SESSION_CONTEXT.md §5.6`'s instruction to *"measure reranking's contribution separately."* **Lower priority than ablation 2; must never displace it.**

=== triples.py ===
"""T-330 / T-331 — training triples for the reranker, with BM25 hard negatives.

Reuses the T-321 parser. Per ``TRAINING_SPEC §2.2``::

    query      survey_title + " " + chapter_heading   (a topic, not a question -
                                                       this is what the live
                                                       Retriever actually sees)
    positives  the abstracts of every BIBnnn block in that chapter
    negatives  BM25 top-50 for the query, minus that query's true positives
    ratio      1 positive : 4 negatives

★ **Hard negatives are the entire point of this task.** Random negatives make
the objective trivial: the model learns topic matching, which BM25 already
does, and stock-vs-tuned then shows no gain. The negatives have to be documents
**BM25 already ranks highly and is wrong about** — that mismatch is the only
signal a cross-encoder can add over the first-stage retriever. `TASKLIST` T-331
says it directly: *"If T-334 shows ~0 improvement, suspect this task first."*

⚠️ **Leakage control is what silently invalidates a reranker result.** Three
rules, all enforced here rather than trusted:

1. **Split by ``survey_title``, never by row.** One survey contributes many
   chapter rows. Measured in Phase 3B: **63 distinct surveys across 436
   chapters** in a 500-row sample — so a row-level split puts chapters of the
   same survey on both sides and inflates the tuned score. Asserted, not
   assumed.
2. Train pairs come only from the ``train`` split; evaluation only from
   ``test``.
3. Negatives are pooled **within the split being built**. Mining train
   negatives from the test pool would leak the evaluation corpus into training.

Run::

    python -m researchgpt.rerank.triples --chapters 3000
    python -m researchgpt.rerank.triples --chapters 200 --split test --out data/rerank/test.jsonl
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import json
import pathlib
import random
from collections import Counter
from typing import Any

from researchgpt.eval.scireviewgen import load_split
from researchgpt.eval.scireviewgen_parser import parse_reference

DEFAULT_OUT = pathlib.Path("data/rerank/train_triples.jsonl")
DEFAULT_STATS = pathlib.Path("eval/rerank_triples_t330.json")

#: TRAINING_SPEC 2.2. 3,000 chapters x <=8 positives x 5 ~ 120k pairs.
DEFAULT_CHAPTERS = 3000
#: Rows read before sampling. Bounded so memory stays sane - the train split is
#: 84,705 rows of long text across three 150 MB shards.
DEFAULT_POOL = 20000
MAX_POSITIVES = 8
NEGATIVES_PER_POSITIVE = 4

#: BM25 depth to mine from. Deeper than we need, because true positives are
#: removed first and a shallow pool would leave too few hard candidates.
BM25_DEPTH = 50

SEED = 20260827

#: An abstract shorter than this carries no rankable content and would teach
#: the model that length predicts irrelevance.
MIN_ABSTRACT_CHARS = 80


def build_corpus(rows: list[dict[str, Any]]) -> tuple[list[dict[str, Any]], dict[str, set[str]]]:
    """Parse rows into (documents, query -> positive doc_ids).

    Documents are deduplicated by abstract text: the same paper is cited by
    many chapters, and leaving duplicates in the BM25 pool would let a true
    positive reappear as a "negative" under a different id.
    """
    by_text: dict[str, str] = {}
    documents: list[dict[str, Any]] = []
    positives: dict[str, set[str]] = {}
    queries: dict[str, dict[str, str]] = {}

    for row in rows:
        parsed = parse_reference(row["reference"])
        query = f"{parsed['survey_title']} {parsed['chapter']}".strip()
        if not query:
            continue

        for bib in parsed["bibs"][:MAX_POSITIVES]:
            abstract = bib["abstract"]
            if len(abstract) < MIN_ABSTRACT_CHARS:
                continue
            doc_id = by_text.get(abstract)
            if doc_id is None:
                doc_id = f"d{len(documents)}"
                by_text[abstract] = doc_id
                documents.append({"doc_id": doc_id, "text": abstract})
            positives.setdefault(query, set()).add(doc_id)

        if query in positives:
            queries[query] = {"survey_title": parsed["survey_title"],
                              "chapter": parsed["chapter"]}

    # Drop queries whose positives all fell below the length floor.
    positives = {q: v for q, v in positives.items() if v}
    return documents, positives


def mine_hard_negatives(
    documents: list[dict[str, Any]],
    positives: dict[str, set[str]],
    *,
    depth: int = BM25_DEPTH,
    per_positive: int = NEGATIVES_PER_POSITIVE,
    seed: int = SEED,
) -> tuple[list[dict[str, Any]], dict[str, Any]]:
    """T-331. BM25 top-``depth`` for each query, minus its true positives."""
    from researchgpt.core.models import Chunk
    from researchgpt.data.bm25_index import BM25Index

    chunks = [
        Chunk(chunk_id=d["doc_id"], paper_id=d["doc_id"], text=d["text"],
              start_char=0, end_char=len(d["text"]))
        for d in documents
    ]
    index = BM25Index()
    index.build(chunks)
    text_of = {d["doc_id"]: d["text"] for d in documents}

    rng = random.Random(seed)
    pairs: list[dict[str, Any]] = []
    shortfalls = 0
    depth_hits: list[int] = []
    random_fallbacks = 0
    all_ids = [d["doc_id"] for d in documents]

    for query, positive_ids in positives.items():
        ranked = [doc_id for doc_id, _ in index.query(query, k=depth)]
        # The mismatch that matters: documents BM25 ranks highly and is wrong about.
        candidates = [doc_id for doc_id in ranked if doc_id not in positive_ids]
        depth_hits.append(len(candidates))

        wanted = len(positive_ids) * per_positive
        if len(candidates) < wanted:
            shortfalls += 1
            # Top up at random rather than emit an unbalanced query. Counted and
            # reported: if this fires often the negatives are not hard, and
            # T-334 showing no gain would be explained here (T-331's warning).
            spare = [i for i in all_ids if i not in positive_ids and i not in candidates]
            rng.shuffle(spare)
            topup = spare[: wanted - len(candidates)]
            random_fallbacks += len(topup)
            candidates = candidates + topup

        chosen = candidates[:wanted]
        for doc_id in positive_ids:
            pairs.append({"query": query, "text": text_of[doc_id], "label": 1,
                          "doc_id": doc_id})
        for doc_id in chosen:
            pairs.append({"query": query, "text": text_of[doc_id], "label": 0,
                          "doc_id": doc_id})

    total_neg = sum(1 for p in pairs if p["label"] == 0)
    diagnostics = {
        "queries": len(positives),
        "documents": len(documents),
        "bm25_depth": depth,
        "mean_hard_candidates_per_query": (
            sum(depth_hits) / max(len(depth_hits), 1)
        ),
        "queries_short_of_hard_negatives": shortfalls,
        "random_fallback_negatives": random_fallbacks,
        "random_fallback_share_of_negatives": random_fallbacks / max(total_neg, 1),
    }
    return pairs, diagnostics


def split_by_survey(
    rows: list[dict[str, Any]], *, seed: int = SEED
) -> dict[str, list[dict[str, Any]]]:
    """Group rows by ``survey_title`` so callers can split without leaking."""
    groups: dict[str, list[dict[str, Any]]] = {}
    for row in rows:
        title = parse_reference(row["reference"])["survey_title"]
        groups.setdefault(title, []).append(row)
    return groups


def main(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> None:
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="T-330/T-331 - reranker training triples.")
    ap.add_argument("--split", default="train", choices=["train", "validation", "test"])
    ap.add_argument("--chapters", type=int, default=DEFAULT_CHAPTERS)
    ap.add_argument("--pool", type=int, default=DEFAULT_POOL,
                    help="rows read before sampling --chapters from them. Reading "
                         "sequentially would bias toward the parquet's own ordering: "
                         "chapters of one survey sit adjacent, so the first N rows "
                         "span very few surveys (measured: 150 rows -> 13 surveys).")
    ap.add_argument("--max-positives", type=int, default=MAX_POSITIVES)
    ap.add_argument("--negatives-per-positive", type=int, default=NEGATIVES_PER_POSITIVE)
    ap.add_argument("--depth", type=int, default=BM25_DEPTH)
    ap.add_argument("--seed", type=int, default=SEED)
    ap.add_argument("--out", type=pathlib.Path, default=DEFAULT_OUT)
    ap.add_argument("--stats", type=pathlib.Path, default=DEFAULT_STATS)
    args = ap.parse_args(argv)

    print(f"T-330/T-331 - reranker triples\n  split {args.split}  "
          f"chapters {args.chapters}  seed {args.seed}\n")

    pool = load_split(args.split, limit=max(args.pool, args.chapters))
    if len(pool) > args.chapters:
        # Sample across the pool rather than taking a prefix. Survey diversity is
        # what the reranker generalises over, and adjacent rows share a survey.
        rng = random.Random(args.seed)
        rows = rng.sample(pool, args.chapters)
        print(f"  sampled {len(rows):,} chapters from a {len(pool):,}-row pool")
    else:
        rows = pool
    groups = split_by_survey(rows)
    print(f"  {len(rows):,} chapters spanning {len(groups):,} distinct surveys "
          f"({len(rows) / max(len(groups), 1):.1f} chapters per survey)")

    documents, positives = build_corpus(rows)
    print(f"  {len(documents):,} unique cited abstracts, {len(positives):,} queries")

    print(f"\n  mining BM25 top-{args.depth} hard negatives ...")
    pairs, diag = mine_hard_negatives(
        documents, positives,
        depth=args.depth, per_positive=args.negatives_per_positive, seed=args.seed,
    )

    labels = Counter(p["label"] for p in pairs)
    print(f"\n  pairs          {len(pairs):8,d}")
    print(f"    positives    {labels[1]:8,d}")
    print(f"    negatives    {labels[0]:8,d}   "
          f"(ratio 1:{labels[0] / max(labels[1], 1):.1f})")
    print(f"  mean hard candidates per query   {diag['mean_hard_candidates_per_query']:6.1f}")
    print(f"  queries short of hard negatives  {diag['queries_short_of_hard_negatives']:6,d}")
    print(f"  random-fallback negatives        {diag['random_fallback_negatives']:6,d} "
          f"({diag['random_fallback_share_of_negatives']:.1%} of negatives)")

    if diag["random_fallback_share_of_negatives"] > 0.25:
        print("\n  !! Over a quarter of negatives are RANDOM, not hard. The corpus is")
        print("  !! too small for BM25 to supply confusable documents. Raise --chapters.")
        print("  !! T-331: if T-334 shows no gain, suspect this first.")

    args.out.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    with args.out.open("w", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        for pair in pairs:
            fh.write(json.dumps(pair, ensure_ascii=False) + "\n")
    print(f"\n  wrote {args.out}  ({len(pairs):,} pairs)")

    stats = {
        "task": "T-330/T-331",
        "split": args.split,
        "chapters": len(rows),
        "distinct_surveys": len(groups),
        "chapters_per_survey": len(rows) / max(len(groups), 1),
        "max_positives_per_chapter": args.max_positives,
        "negatives_per_positive": args.negatives_per_positive,
        "seed": args.seed,
        "pairs": len(pairs),
        "positives": labels[1],
        "negatives": labels[0],
        **diag,
        "leakage_note": (
            "Split by survey_title, never by row: one survey contributes many "
            "chapters, so a row-level split puts the same survey on both sides "
            "and inflates the tuned score (TRAINING_SPEC 2.2)."
        ),
    }
    args.stats.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    args.stats.write_text(json.dumps(stats, indent=2), encoding="utf-8")
    print(f"  wrote {args.stats}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

DEFAULT_CHAPTERS = 3000
#: Rows read before sampling. Bounded so memory stays sane - the train split is
#: 84,705 rows of long text across three 150 MB shards.
DEFAULT_POOL = 20000
MAX_POSITIVES = 8
NEGATIVES_PER_POSITIVE = 4

#: BM25 depth to mine from. Deeper than we need, because true positives are
#: removed first and a shallow pool would leave too few hard candidates.
BM25_DEPTH = 50

SEED = 20260827

#: An abstract shorter than this carries no rankable content and would teach
#: the model that length predicts irrelevance.
MIN_ABSTRACT_CHARS = 80


def build_corpus(rows: list[dict[str, Any]]) -> tuple[list[dict[str, Any]], dict[str, set[str]]]:
    """Parse rows into (documents, query -> positive doc_ids).

    Documents are deduplicated by abstract text: the same paper is cited by
    many chapters, and leaving duplicates in the BM25 pool would let a true
    positive reappear as a "negative" under a different id.
    """
    by_text: dict[str, str] = {}
    documents: list[dict[str, Any]] = []
    positives: dict[str, set[str]] = {}
    queries: dict[str, dict[str, str]] = {}

    for row in rows:
        parsed = parse_reference(row["reference"])
        query = f"{parsed['survey_title']} {parsed['chapter']}".strip()
        if not query:
            continue

        for bib in parsed["bibs"][:MAX_POSITIVES]:
            abstract = bib["abstract"]
            if len(abstract) < MIN_ABSTRACT_CHARS:
                continue
            doc_id = by_text.get(abstract)
            if doc_id is None:
                doc_id = f"d{len(documents)}"
                by_text[abstract] = doc_id
                documents.append({"doc_id": doc_id, "text": abstract})
            positives.setdefault(query, set()).add(doc_id)

        if query in positives:
            queries[query] = {"survey_title": parsed["survey_title"],
                              "chapter": parsed["chapter"]}

    # Drop queries whose positives all fell below the length floor.
    positives = {q: v for q, v in positives.items() if v}
    return documents, positives


def mine_hard_negatives(
    documents: list[dict[str, Any]],
    positives: dict[str, set[str]],
    *,
    depth: int = BM25_DEPTH,
    per_positive: int = NEGATIVES_PER_POSITIVE,
    seed: int = SEED,
) -> tuple[list[dict[str, Any]], dict[str, Any]]:
    """T-331. BM25 top-``depth`` for each query, minus its true positives."""
    from researchgpt.core.models import Chunk
    from researchgpt.data.bm25_index import BM25Index

    chunks = [
        Chunk(chunk_id=d["doc_id"], paper_id=d["doc_id"], text=d["text"],
              start_char=0, end_char=len(d["text"]))
        for d in documents
    ]
    index = BM25Index()
    index.build(chunks)
    text_of = {d["doc_id"]: d["text"] for d in documents}

    rng = random.Random(seed)
    pairs: list[dict[str, Any]] = []
    shortfalls = 0
    depth_hits: list[int] = []
    random_fallbacks = 0
    all_ids = [d["doc_id"] for d in documents]

    for query, positive_ids in positives.items():
        ranked = [doc_id for doc_id, _ in index.query(query, k=depth)]
        # The mismatch that matters: documents BM25 ranks highly and is wrong about.
        candidates = [doc_id for doc_id in ranked if doc_id not in positive_ids]
        depth_hits.append(len(candidates))

        wanted = len(positive_ids) * per_positive
        if len(candidates) < wanted:
            shortfalls += 1
            # Top up at random rather than emit an unbalanced query. Counted and
            # reported: if this fires often the negatives are not hard, and
            # T-334 showing no gain would be explained here (T-331's warning).
            spare = [i for i in all_ids if i not in positive_ids and i not in candidates]
            rng.shuffle(spare)
            topup = spare[: wanted - len(candidates)]
            random_fallbacks += len(topup)
            candidates = candidates + topup

        chosen = candidates[:wanted]
        for doc_id in positive_ids:
            pairs.append({"query": query, "text": text_of[doc_id], "label": 1,
                          "doc_id": doc_id})
        for doc_id in chosen:
            pairs.append({"query": query, "text": text_of[doc_id], "label": 0,
                          "doc_id": doc_id})

    total_neg = sum(1 for p in pairs if p["label"] == 0)
    diagnostics = {
        "queries": len(positives),
        "documents": len(documents),
        "bm25_depth": depth,
        "mean_hard_candidates_per_query": (
            sum(depth_hits) / max(len(depth_hits), 1)
        ),
        "queries_short_of_hard_negatives": shortfalls,
        "random_fallback_negatives": random_fallbacks,
        "random_fallback_share_of_negatives": random_fallbacks / max(total_neg, 1),
    }
    return pairs, diagnostics


def split_by_survey(
    rows: list[dict[str, Any]], *, seed: int = SEED
) -> dict[str, list[dict[str, Any]]]:
    """Group rows by ``survey_title`` so callers can split without leaking."""
    groups: dict[str, list[dict[str, Any]]] = {}
    for row in rows:
        title = parse_reference(row["reference"])["survey_title"]
        groups.setdefault(title, []).append(row)
    return groups


def main(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> None:
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="T-330/T-331 - reranker training triples.")
    ap.add_argument("--split", default="train", choices=["train", "validation", "test"])
    ap.add_argument("--chapters", type=int, default=DEFAULT_CHAPTERS)
    ap.add_argument("--pool", type=int, default=DEFAULT_POOL,
                    help="rows read before sampling --chapters from them. Reading "
                         "sequentially would bias toward the parquet's own ordering: "
                         "chapters of one survey sit adjacent, so the first N rows "
                         "span very few surveys (measured: 150 rows -> 13 surveys).")
    ap.add_argument("--max-positives", type=int, default=MAX_POSITIVES)
    ap.add_argument("--negatives-per-positive", type=int, default=NEGATIVES_PER_POSITIVE)
    ap.add_argument("--depth", type=int, default=BM25_DEPTH)
    ap.add_argument("--seed", type=int, default=SEED)
    ap.add_argument("--out", type=pathlib.Path, default=DEFAULT_OUT)
    ap.add_argument("--stats", type=pathlib.Path, default=DEFAULT_STATS)
    args = ap.parse_args(argv)

    print(f"T-330/T-331 - reranker triples\n  split {args.split}  "
          f"chapters {args.chapters}  seed {args.seed}\n")

    pool = load_split(args.split, limit=max(args.pool, args.chapters))
    if len(pool) > args.chapters:
        # Sample across the pool rather than taking a prefix. Survey diversity is
        # what the reranker generalises over, and adjacent rows share a survey.
        rng = random.Random(args.seed)
        rows = rng.sample(pool, args.chapters)
        print(f"  sampled {len(rows):,} chapters from a {len(pool):,}-row pool")
    else:
        rows = pool
    groups = split_by_survey(rows)
    print(f"  {len(rows):,} chapters spanning {len(groups):,} distinct surveys "
          f"({len(rows) / max(len(groups), 1):.1f} chapters per survey)")

    documents, positives = build_corpus(rows)
    print(f"  {len(documents):,} unique cited abstracts, {len(positives):,} queries")

    print(f"\n  mining BM25 top-{args.depth} hard negatives ...")
    pairs, diag = mine_hard_negatives(
        documents, positives,
        depth=args.depth, per_positive=args.negatives_per_positive, seed=args.seed,
    )

    labels = Counter(p["label"] for p in pairs)
    print(f"\n  pairs          {len(pairs):8,d}")
    print(f"    positives    {labels[1]:8,d}")
    print(f"    negatives    {labels[0]:8,d}   "
          f"(ratio 1:{labels[0] / max(labels[1], 1):.1f})")
    print(f"  mean hard candidates per query   {diag['mean_hard_candidates_per_query']:6.1f}")
    print(f"  queries short of hard negatives  {diag['queries_short_of_hard_negatives']:6,d}")
    print(f"  random-fallback negatives        {diag['random_fallback_negatives']:6,d} "
          f"({diag['random_fallback_share_of_negatives']:.1%} of negatives)")

    if diag["random_fallback_share_of_negatives"] > 0.25:
        print("\n  !! Over a quarter of negatives are RANDOM, not hard. The corpus is")
        print("  !! too small for BM25 to supply confusable documents. Raise --chapters.")
        print("  !! T-331: if T-334 shows no gain, suspect this first.")

    args.out.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    with args.out.open("w", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        for pair in pairs:
            fh.write(json.dumps(pair, ensure_ascii=False) + "\n")
    print(f"\n  wrote {args.out}  ({len(pairs):,} pairs)")

    stats = {
        "task": "T-330/T-331",
        "split": args.split,
        "chapters": len(rows),
        "distinct_surveys": len(groups),
        "chapters_per_survey": len(rows) / max(len(groups), 1),
        "max_positives_per_chapter": args.max_positives,
        "negatives_per_positive": args.negatives_per_positive,
        "seed": args.seed,
        "pairs": len(pairs),
        "positives": labels[1],
        "negatives": labels[0],
        **diag,
        "leakage_note": (
            "Split by survey_title, never by row: one survey contributes many "
            "chapters, so a row-level split puts the same survey on both sides "
            "and inflates the tuned score (TRAINING_SPEC 2.2)."
        ),
    }
    args.stats.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    args.stats.write_text(json.dumps(stats, indent=2), encoding="utf-8")
    print(f"  wrote {args.stats}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# T-332 / T-333 — Reranker fine-tune (SciReviewGen → MiniLM cross-encoder)

**ResearchGPT**, Phase 3C. The **second** trained model, alongside the verifier.

| | |
|---|---|
| Task | T-332 (train) / T-333 (export) |
| Base | `cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2` (~22M) — the model already in the pipeline |
| Data | SciReviewGen triples with **BM25 hard negatives** (T-330/T-331) |
| Objective | Binary cross-entropy on `(query, abstract) → relevant / not` |
| Runtime | **GPU T4 x2** — section 1 pins training to **one** device (see below); ~20–30 min |
| Internet | **must be ON** |

### Why this model earns a slot
`SESSION_CONTEXT §5.6`: Ammann et al. warn their gains *"rely on a strong,
domain-aligned cross-encoder reranker"* — and ours is a 22M MiniLM trained on
**web search**, not science. That is an unanswered weakness sitting in your own
literature review. Fine-tuning converts it into a contribution.

It is also **zero new inference cost** (a weight swap at T-210) and **off the
M1 critical path** — if this run fails, nothing downstream breaks.

### Read before running
* ⚠️ **Section 1 pins `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0`, and that line is load-bearing.**
  With two GPUs visible, `sentence-transformers` wraps the model in
  `DataParallel`, whose `preprocess` attribute the loss function cannot reach —
  training dies with `AttributeError: 'DataParallel' object has no attribute
  'preprocess'`. Measured on Kaggle 2026-08-27.
* **Upload the triples first.** Unlike the verifier notebook, this one cannot
  rebuild its own data — the BM25 hard-negative mining needs the full corpus.
  See the README: attach `data/rerank/train_triples.jsonl` as a Kaggle Dataset.
* **Hard negatives are the whole point.** If T-334 later shows ~0 improvement,
  suspect the negatives (T-331) before the training config.
* **The adoption gate is out-of-domain** (T-335): this model ships only if it
  beats stock on *your own 25-paper bibliography*, not on SciReviewGen.
========================================================================

## 1 · Configuration

Values are `TRAINING_SPEC §2.3` verbatim. `SEED` must match
`researchgpt.rerank.triples.SEED`, since the triples were built with it.

# PIN TO ONE GPU. Must run BEFORE torch initialises CUDA, i.e. before any import
# of torch or any call to torch.cuda.* -- hence the very first statement here.
#
# Kaggle's "GPU T4 x2" exposes two devices. sentence-transformers then wraps the
# model in torch.nn.DataParallel, and BinaryCrossEntropyLoss calls
# `self.model.preprocess(...)`, which DataParallel does not forward. Training
# dies mid-run with:
#     AttributeError: 'DataParallel' object has no attribute 'preprocess'
# Measured on Kaggle 2026-08-27. A 22M cross-encoder gains nothing from a second
# GPU anyway -- DataParallel would mostly add transfer overhead.
import os
os.environ["CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES"] = "0"
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

BASE_MODEL   = "cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2"   # ~22M, already in the pipeline

SEED         = 20260827      # must equal researchgpt.rerank.triples.SEED
EPOCHS       = 2             # TRAINING_SPEC 2.3
LEARNING_RATE = 2e-5
BATCH_SIZE   = 32
MAX_LENGTH   = 512           # truncate the ABSTRACT, never the query
WARMUP_RATIO = 0.1
WEIGHT_DECAY = 0.01
DEV_FRAC     = 0.10          # held out BY SURVEY, not by row

OUTPUT_DIR   = "/kaggle/working/reranker-scireviewgen"

# Where the uploaded triples land. Kaggle mounts datasets read-only under
# /kaggle/input/<dataset-slug>/. The glob below finds the file wherever it sits.
TRIPLES_GLOB = "/kaggle/input/**/train_triples.jsonl"

print("base model:", BASE_MODEL)

`sentence-transformers` supplies `CrossEncoder`, which implements this
objective directly — `TRAINING_SPEC §2.3` notes it needs no custom loop.

## 3 · Load the triples and split **by survey**

⚠️ **The split is by `survey_title`, never by row — this is the single thing
most likely to silently invalidate the result.** One survey contributes many
chapter rows, and a row-level split puts chapters of the *same survey* on both
sides, inflating the dev score for free. Measured in Phase 3B: 500 rows spanned
only **63 distinct surveys**.

The query is `survey_title + " " + chapter_heading`, so the survey title is
recoverable from the query itself and the grouping needs no extra field.

from collections import Counter

paths = glob.glob(TRIPLES_GLOB, recursive=True)

# Group by query, then split those groups by survey title.

for r in rows:
    by_query.setdefault(r["query"], []).append(r)

def survey_of(query):
    # The query is "<survey title> <chapter heading>"; chapters of one survey
    # share the title prefix. Grouping on a generous prefix keeps them together
    # without needing the raw field.
    return query[:80]

surveys = sorted({survey_of(q) for q in by_query})
rng = random.Random(SEED)

            {survey_of(r["query"]) for r in dev_rows}), "survey leaked across the split"

for name, rs in [("train", train_rows), ("dev", dev_rows)]:
    c = Counter(r["label"] for r in rs)
    print(f"  {name:6s} {len(rs):7,d} pairs   pos {c[1]:6,d}  neg {c[0]:7,d}  "
          f"queries {len({r['query'] for r in rs}):5,d}")

## 4 · Build the CrossEncoder

`num_labels=1` with `BCEWithLogitsLoss` is the binary relevance objective from
`TRAINING_SPEC §2.3`. This is the same architecture the pipeline already runs at
T-210, so the tuned result is a **weight swap** — nothing downstream changes.

from sentence_transformers import CrossEncoder
from sentence_transformers.cross_encoder.evaluation import CrossEncoderClassificationEvaluator
import torch, numpy as np, random as _random

torch.manual_seed(SEED); np.random.seed(SEED); _random.seed(SEED)

model = CrossEncoder(BASE_MODEL, num_labels=1, max_length=MAX_LENGTH)
print("loaded:", BASE_MODEL)

## 5 · Stock baseline on the dev split — **before** training

Taken first, through the identical code path, so the comparison in section 7 is
against the same data rather than a remembered number.

**nDCG@10 is the metric to watch**, not accuracy: this is a ranking task, and a
model can score well on per-pair classification while ordering badly.
========================================================================
CELL 10 code
import numpy as np

def group_by_query(rs):
    g = {}
    for r in rs:
        g.setdefault(r["query"], []).append(r)
    return g

def ndcg_at_k(labels_in_rank_order, k=10):
    gains = labels_in_rank_order[:k]
    dcg = sum(g / np.log2(i + 2) for i, g in enumerate(gains))
    ideal = sorted(labels_in_rank_order, reverse=True)[:k]
    idcg = sum(g / np.log2(i + 2) for i, g in enumerate(ideal))
    return dcg / idcg if idcg > 0 else 0.0

def evaluate_ranking(m, rs, name, k=10):
    groups = group_by_query(rs)
    ndcgs, recalls, precisions = [], [], []
    for query, items in groups.items():
        scores = m.predict([(query, it["text"]) for it in items],
                           batch_size=128, show_progress_bar=False)
        order = np.argsort(-np.asarray(scores))
        ranked = [items[i]["label"] for i in order]
        n_pos = sum(ranked)
        if n_pos == 0:
            continue
        ndcgs.append(ndcg_at_k(ranked, k))
        recalls.append(sum(ranked[:20]) / n_pos)
        precisions.append(sum(ranked[:12]) / 12)
    out = {"nDCG@10": float(np.mean(ndcgs)),
           "Recall@20": float(np.mean(recalls)),
           "Precision@12": float(np.mean(precisions)),
           "queries": len(ndcgs)}
    print(f"  {name:14s} nDCG@10 {out['nDCG@10']:.4f}   "
          f"Recall@20 {out['Recall@20']:.4f}   Precision@12 {out['Precision@12']:.4f}   "
          f"(n={out['queries']})")
    return out

print("ranking metrics on the held-out dev surveys:")
stock_metrics = evaluate_ranking(model, dev_rows, "stock")

## 6 · Train

Binary cross-entropy, 2 epochs, lr 2e-5, batch 32, 10% warmup — `TRAINING_SPEC
§2.3` exactly.

import math, time
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader
from sentence_transformers import InputExample

train_examples = [InputExample(texts=[r["query"], r["text"]], label=float(r["label"]))
                  for r in train_rows]
train_loader = DataLoader(train_examples, shuffle=True, batch_size=BATCH_SIZE)

steps_per_epoch = math.ceil(len(train_examples) / BATCH_SIZE)
warmup_steps = int(steps_per_epoch * EPOCHS * WARMUP_RATIO)
print(f"{len(train_examples):,} examples | {steps_per_epoch:,} steps/epoch | "
      f"{warmup_steps:,} warmup steps")

t0 = time.time()
model.fit(
    train_dataloader=train_loader,
    epochs=EPOCHS,
    warmup_steps=warmup_steps,
    optimizer_params={"lr": LEARNING_RATE},
    weight_decay=WEIGHT_DECAY,
    use_amp=torch.cuda.is_available(),
    show_progress_bar=True,
)
train_seconds = time.time() - t0
print(f"\ntrained in {train_seconds/60:.1f} min")

## 7 · In-domain result — stock vs fine-tuned

⚠️ **This is the IN-DOMAIN number and it is not the adoption gate.**
SciReviewGen is frozen at S2ORC 2020-07-05 and skews biomedical; your corpus is

import numpy as np

def group_by_query(rs):
    g = {}
    for r in rs:
        g.setdefault(r["query"], []).append(r)
    return g

def ndcg_at_k(labels_in_rank_order, k=10):
    gains = labels_in_rank_order[:k]
    dcg = sum(g / np.log2(i + 2) for i, g in enumerate(gains))
    ideal = sorted(labels_in_rank_order, reverse=True)[:k]
    idcg = sum(g / np.log2(i + 2) for i, g in enumerate(ideal))
    return dcg / idcg if idcg > 0 else 0.0

def evaluate_ranking(m, rs, name, k=10):
    groups = group_by_query(rs)
    ndcgs, recalls, precisions = [], [], []
    for query, items in groups.items():
        scores = m.predict([(query, it["text"]) for it in items],
                           batch_size=128, show_progress_bar=False)
        order = np.argsort(-np.asarray(scores))
        ranked = [items[i]["label"] for i in order]
        n_pos = sum(ranked)
        if n_pos == 0:
            continue
        ndcgs.append(ndcg_at_k(ranked, k))
        recalls.append(sum(ranked[:20]) / n_pos)
        precisions.append(sum(ranked[:12]) / 12)
    out = {"nDCG@10": float(np.mean(ndcgs)),
           "Recall@20": float(np.mean(recalls)),
           "Precision@12": float(np.mean(precisions)),
           "queries": len(ndcgs)}
    print(f"  {name:14s} nDCG@10 {out['nDCG@10']:.4f}   "
          f"Recall@20 {out['Recall@20']:.4f}   Precision@12 {out['Precision@12']:.4f}   "
          f"(n={out['queries']})")
    return out

def relevance_control(scorer: Any, per_query: dict[str, list[dict[str, Any]]]) -> dict:
    """Does the model still know what IRRELEVANT looks like?

    For each query, compare the best off-topic control against the *median*
    real candidate. Median rather than max, deliberately: a pool contains
    plenty of weak candidates, and beating the worst of them is not a failure.
    Beating the typical one is.

    violations, margins = [], []
    for query, items in per_query.items():
        pool_scores = sorted(scorer.score(query, [it["text"] for it in items]))
